sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to rest in the seventh year from the work of the field. This mitzva is like the mitzva of Shabbat, except that on the seventh day one rests from all work, and in the seventh year one rests from the work of the field. From the mitzva of resting several mitzvot follow: one, the release of the produce that grows in the shemita year, that is, declaring it ownerless for everyone. Second, care with the produce of Shevi'it, which is sanctified for eating, and it is forbidden to waste it and forbidden to trade in it. Third, similar to the release of the produce, there is a mitzva to release debts at the end of the seventh year, that is, to forgo the debts that have not been paid.

And so it is clear from the language of the Torah that the main mitzva is to rest, and only from this follows the mitzva of declaring the produce ownerless and sanctifying it for eating. As it is said (Vayikra 25:2-7): "When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall rest a Sabbath to the Lord. Six years you shall sow your field, and six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its produce. But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the Lord; you shall not sow your field and you shall not prune your vineyard. That which grows of itself from your harvest you shall not reap, and the grapes of your untended vine you shall not gather; it shall be a year of solemn rest for the land. And the Sabbath of the land shall be for you for food: for you, and for your servant and for your maidservant, and for your hired worker and for your resident who sojourn with you. And for your cattle and for the beasts that are in your land shall all its produce be for food."

Admittedly, some hold that the main aim of Shevi'it is that everyone should eat equally from the produce. But in practice, following the prohibition of sowing and pruning, the produce of Shevi'it was very limited; for usually a considerable majority of the produce of the fields is from annual crops of grain, legumes and vegetables, and they do not exist at all in Shevi'it because of the prohibition of sowing and planting. And even the amount of fruit that grew on the trees diminished, since it is forbidden to prune and to do work that helps their growth. One can estimate that the produce that grew by itself in Shevi'it was about 20% of the produce of the other years; thus the main mitzva is to rest (below 3:1).

The resting is to Hashem. The Sages said (Sanhedrin 39a): "The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: Sow six and release the seventh, so that you will know that the land is Mine." And this was a very hard trial, for the main livelihood was from the work of the field, and the Torah commanded Israel to believe in Hashem that although they would rest from the work of their fields for a whole year, they would merit blessing in the other years and their households would not hunger for bread. The Sages said that about those who keep Shevi'it it is said (Tehillim 103:20): "Bless the Lord, His angels, mighty in strength, who do His word, hearkening to the voice of His word." For throughout a whole year, day after day, month after month, they see their fields ownerless and their gates broken open, their trees ownerless and their fruit eaten, and they conquer their inclination and keep silent (Vayikra Rabba 1:1; Tanḥuma there 1).

The resting in the seventh year should create in the consciousness of Israel an empty space that will be filled with faith in Hashem, that the whole land belongs to Him, and out of this blessing will be drawn to the six years of work. For a considerable part of the time that became free was meant, of course, for Torah study, to fulfil what is said (Yehoshua 1:8): "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may take care to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall succeed" (below 5). Out of the resting and the study, inspiration was drawn for the improvement and development of the work during the following six years (below 7-8; 11:7-8).

sections.title_en: 2. The Release of the Produce and Its Holiness
sections.body_en:
As a continuation and completion of the mitzva of resting, we were commanded to declare ownerless the produce that grows in Shevi'it, so that everyone may eat from it, the owner of the field like other people, poor and rich, human beings and animals. As it is said (Shemot 23:10-11): "And six years you shall sow your land and gather in its produce. But the seventh year you shall release it and let it lie, so that the poor of your people may eat, and what they leave the beast of the field shall eat; so shall you do with your vineyard and with your olive grove." The Sages said (Mekhilta de-Rashbi there) that the owner of the field may not guard the produce of his field in order to distribute it equally to everyone or to the poor, because it is said "and let it lie", that it should be ownerless for everyone. And what is said, "so that the poor of your people may eat", is because usually the poor would eat most of the produce, for it was worthwhile for them to take the trouble to come to the orchards and pick the fruit for their household's consumption; but if the rich wished, they too could eat from the produce (below 3:1).

Thus the produce of Shevi'it that grew by itself is Hashem's, and therefore the Torah commanded the owners of the fields to open their fields to everyone, in order to fulfil through the produce the Divine will to sustain every living thing. Through this the owner of the field will merit to cleave to the attribute of the Holy One, blessed be He, of whom it is said (Tehillim 145:16): "You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favour." And he will also merit to acquire the trait of yielding, for there is none more generous than one who gives without expecting a return (Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh 84; below 3:2).

Since the produce of Shevi'it is Hashem's, one must treat it with holiness, not changing it from its original purpose: it is to be for eating and not for waste, for eating and not for trade. As it is said (Vayikra 25:6-7): "And the Sabbath of the land shall be for you for food: for you, and for your servant and for your maidservant, and for your hired worker and for your resident who sojourn with you. And for your cattle and for the beasts that are in your land shall all its produce be for food." In all the years the produce belongs to the owner of the field, and he may use it for all his needs. In this way the produce loses its own value and becomes a tool in the hand of the owner, who can trade in it to earn money and buy with it everything his heart desires. When it is useful to him, he may also waste the produce, or make from it a decoration or glue, or take grasses intended as animal food and fire the oven with them to heat his house. But with the produce of Shevi'it all these things are forbidden: since the produce is Hashem's, it returns to its original purpose, to be food for every living thing. And this is the meaning of the holiness with which we were commanded to treat the produce of Shevi'it (as explained in chapter 4).

A person may take produce of Shevi'it only for the food of his household; and if produce remained in his house when the produce in the field has run out, so that the wild animals can no longer eat of it, he is obligated to remove the produce from his house and distribute it to everyone or declare it ownerless; and this is the mitzva of bi'ur (removal) of the produce of Shevi'it (below 4:10-11).

As a continuation of the release of the produce during the shemita year, we were commanded to release at the end of the year the debts that our brethren, the children of Israel, owe us. As it is said (Devarim 15:1-2): "At the end of every seven years you shall make a release. And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his fellow; he shall not exact it of his fellow and of his brother, because the Lord's release has been proclaimed."

The release of money is similar to some extent to the mitzva of returning the fields to their owners in the Yovel (below 9:5). And so too in halakha, the mitzva of Shevi'it and the mitzva of the Yovel depend on each other, and when the mitzva of the Yovel lapsed, the mitzva of Shevi'it too lapsed (Gittin 36a).

This mitzva extends outside the Land: out of the resting of the Land and the release of the produce in the Land of Israel, the mitzva to release debts is drawn also outside the Land. As it is said: "because the Lord's release has been proclaimed" – the proclamation of the release extends to every place (Kiddushin 38b).

The Torah warned not to refrain from lending money to trustworthy people as the shemita year approaches. For since they are people who are accustomed to repay their debt on time, one should not worry excessively that they will not manage to repay the loan on time and it will be released. As it is said (Devarim 15:9-10): "Beware lest there be a base thought in your heart, saying: The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand; and your eye be evil against your needy brother and you give him nothing, and he cry to the Lord against you, and it be sin in you. You shall surely give him, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him, because for this thing the Lord your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you put your hand to."

One should know that the main debts the Torah spoke of are small, short-term debts that people took in order to buy food. As the Sages said (Makkot 3b): an unspecified loan is for thirty days, and its aim is to help a person in his time of need. For it happens that people who work for their livelihood are at times left without money, because they have not finished their work, or because they have not found a buyer for their wares, or because they have not yet been paid; and in order to buy food they were forced to ask for loans. They were not the poor to whom the Torah commanded giving tzedaka; rather they needed a loan that would allow them to survive until they received their wages. And the Torah commanded lending to them sufficient for their need. But there are always a few borrowers whose situation remains so tight that they do not have the strength to pay their debt, and the Torah commanded that at the end of the shemita year the lenders forgo their debt. However, if the borrowers are able, it is a mitzva for them to repay their debt (below 6:2-3).

At the end of the days of the Second Temple, the poor who requested loans and could not repay them became so many that the loss to the lenders was too great, above and beyond what the Torah intended. And so that they could continue to lend without worrying about losses that were too great, Hillel the Elder enacted the prozbul, by which the loans remained in force even after the shemita (as explained below 6:5).

sections.title_en: 4. The Revelation of the Soul in Shabbat and in Shevi'it
sections.body_en:
The Sages said: "The Holy One, blessed be He, created many things in the world and selected for Himself one of them. He created seven days and the Holy One, blessed be He, chose Shabbat, as it is said (Bereshit 2:3): 'And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.' He created years and selected for Himself one of them, as it is said (Vayikra 25:2): 'The land shall rest a Sabbath to the Lord'… He created lands and selected for Himself one of them – the Land of Israel, as it is said (Devarim 11:12): 'The eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it.' And likewise the Holy One, blessed be He, calls it His land, as it is said (Yoel 4:2): 'And they divided My land'… He created nations and selected for Himself one of them – this is Israel, as it is said (Devarim 14:2): 'And the Lord has chosen you to be His treasured people'…" (Bamidbar Rabba 3:8. And in the Zohar vol. 3, Ra'aya Mehemna 108b, all the sevenths are from the side of holiness.)

It is not by chance that Hashem chose the seventh day and the seventh year; rather it is because they are suited to the revelation of inwardness. As the Maharal explained, every physical thing has six sides – up and down and the four directions of the world – and the seventh number expresses its sanctified inwardness (Tiferet Yisrael 40). And the Land of Israel too is the centre of the lands, and the people of Israel relative to the nations is like the heart among the limbs (Kuzari 1:103; 2:14-20; 36; 50).

It turns out that the resting is meant to reveal the inner soul. All the days of the week a person toils at his work and his soul is hidden; and through Shabbat his soul comes to expression and he can delight in Hashem through Torah study and the Shabbat meals, and out of this he understands the value of his work in the six days of action, and it is blessed (see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 1:5-6).

What Shabbat does for each and every individual, the seventh year does for all Israel. Through rest from the toil and preoccupation of the work of the field, the children of Israel are strengthened in faith in Hashem and increase their Torah study. Through declaring the produce ownerless and releasing the debts, the children of Israel are relieved of the tension and competition that accompany trading in produce, and bring out the trait of kindness and compassion between a person and his fellow. And so for a whole year the soul returns to shine in Israel, and they recall all the good aspirations, and long for a world repaired with kindness and truth; the love between neighbours grows stronger, and social life keeps improving. And out of this blessing is drawn to the six years of work (based on the introduction to Shabbat Ha-Aretz).

In our time less than two percent of the whole population in Israel is engaged in agriculture, and it is fitting that the idea of resting in Shevi'it come to expression in all professions, as will be explained below (11:6).

It is a mitzva to increase Torah study in the seventh year, in which one rests from the work of the field, and this mitzva rests on two foundations:

The first is that it would have been fitting for a person to devote many hours every day and every night to study the whole Torah and meditate on it, as it is said (Yehoshua 1:8): "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night." And as we were commanded (Devarim 5:1): "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them"; and likewise it is said (there 6:6-7): "And these words, which I command you this day, shall be upon your heart. And you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down and when you rise up" (see Yoma 19b). But in practice, during the six years in which a person must work in his field, he cannot study a great deal. But in the seventh year, in which we were commanded to rest from the work of the field, the mitzva of Torah study returns to its place in its full force.

And so we learned regarding Shabbat. The Sages said (Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu Rabba 1): "So said the Holy One, blessed be He, to Israel: My children, did I not write thus to you in My Torah: 'This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night'? Even though you do work all six days, the day of Shabbat shall be made entirely Torah." They further said: "The Torah said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, when Israel enter the Land, this one will run to his vineyard and that one will run to his field, and what will become of me? He said to her: I have a partner whom I will pair with you, and Shabbat is its name, for they are idle from their work and can engage in you" (Tur OḤ 290). And just as they said regarding Shabbat, so one must say regarding the seventh year: the resting in it is meant so that Israel will be able to meditate on the Torah, and through this they will merit to reveal the value of work and will be able to endure in the Land.

The second foundation is that Shevi'it is a year in which there is holiness, for its resting is a resting to Hashem, as it is said (Vayikra 25:2-4): "The land shall rest a Sabbath to the Lord… But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the Lord." And just as on Shabbat the holiness comes to expression in Torah study, so in Shevi'it it should come to expression in Torah study (Ibn Ezra; Sforno; and see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 5:1; Festivals 1:5).1

And so they hinted in the Zohar, in describing what takes place in Gan Eden in the shemita: Come and see: in each and every shemita a herald goes out in Gan Eden and says: Gather, men and women, and all those people of faith, and ascend from the lower Gan Eden to the upper Gan Eden. And then all of them strip off their outer garments, males and females, and with them all the little ones and the youths, and they ascend and enter the academy of the firmament, and rejoice there in the joy of their elevation; and there is joy upon joy there, and new and old words of Torah are said there, and all of them there rejoice with a joy like no other (vol. 3, 171b, in translation and explanation).

notes_en.en: The foundations explained here are brought in many books, among them: the long Ibn Ezra, Shemot 20:8; Sforno, Vayikra 25:2-4; Ḥeshek Shlomo on the Kuzari 2:50, by Rabbi Shlomo ben Yehuda of Lunel; Rabbi Ḥaim Vital in Etz Ha-Da'at Tov 150b; the Ḥida in Naḥal Kedumim, Behar 1, and in Penei David, Behar 3; Rav Tzvi Hirsch Kalischer in Sefer Ha-Brit, Vayikra 25:2; the Netziv in Ha'amek Davar, Shemot 34:21; Peri Tzaddik, Mishpatim 2. And likewise it is explained in the introduction to Shabbat Ha-Aretz that Shevi'it is to the nation as Shabbat is to the individual.

sections.body_en:
Through the mitzva of Shevi'it Israel merit to repair the sin of Adam and to redeem man and the earth from their curse. Following the sin, human society became enslaved to obtaining the means of its existence, to the point that all its values were enslaved to this, all its aspirations were directed to improving its material condition, and the soul was hidden and disappeared. As it is said (Bereshit 3:17-19): "Cursed is the ground for your sake; in sorrow you shall eat of it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for dust you are, and to dust you shall return." In this way man can exist, but his existence is painful and exhausting: the existence of a slave forced to give up his selfhood in order to sustain himself and supply his needs and urges. It was not then conceivable that an entire people could exist while resting from all work on the day of Shabbat and resting from the work of the field for a whole year.

And Hashem wished to redeem Israel and the world, and He gave us the Torah and the mitzvot of Shabbat and Shevi'it, through which we connect to the complete state of life, in which we are free from enslavement to hard labour, and the soul is revealed and shines, and out of this we can elevate the world and repair it. And Hashem promised Israel that if they keep the mitzvot they will not lack food, and will even merit abundant blessing. And the more Israel strengthened themselves in keeping Shabbat and Shevi'it, the more the blessing grew.

For this is the right balance: on the one hand a person is obligated to take care of his existence, and therefore he must work in his field diligently, save money and become established, and in this he repairs his sin and overcomes the inclination to laziness. And on the other hand, he must remember Hashem, Creator of heaven and earth, who gave him the strength to work, and in this he repairs the inclination to pride. It seems at first glance that there is a compromise here: from the economic consideration it would have been fitting to work seven years, and from the spiritual consideration it would have been fitting always to rest. In order to strengthen himself in the trait of responsibility and diligence he must work; in order to strengthen himself in the trait of humility and faith he must rest. And as it were, the Torah made a realistic compromise in which a person could survive while giving room to both aspirations.

But the truth is that there is no compromise here, but an expression of two values that fertilise and complement each other. The need to prepare for the day of Shabbat and for the seventh year elevates the value of work and teaches Israel to be more responsible and diligent in the six days of action and the six years of work. And by virtue of these preparations, Israel merit to be elevated and sanctified on Shabbat and in the seventh year; their soul is freed from the yoke of work and the pursuit of the needs of physical existence and the urges that accompany it, and reveals its freedom and connects to Hashem. And out of this Israel understand the true value of their work, to add goodness and blessing to the world; and they develop ways to improve work and make it more efficient, and the world keeps rising, and the blessing of Heaven flows to the earth (see Kuzari 2:50; Otzar Neḥmad there). And so from Shabbat to Shabbat, and from Shevi'it to Shevi'it, Israel are progressively redeemed, until the complete redemption, which too will come out of the seventh year. Therefore the Sages enacted to say the blessing of redemption as the seventh blessing in the Shemoneh Esreh prayer (Megilla 17b).

A great secret lies in the blessing of Shabbat and Shevi'it. As is known, a person's livelihood is hard, so much so that the Sages said (Pesaḥim 118a): "A person's sustenance is as hard as the splitting of the Sea of Reeds." His life depends on his food; if he does not eat for several days he will die of hunger. And a person must work his land by the sweat of his brow and grow grain and fruit to sustain himself. And at times the rains are withheld and the produce is small and people die of hunger, and only those who were wise enough to save find bread to keep their households alive. Therefore it is fitting for every person to work diligently at every occupation, in order to give his household bread to eat, clothing to wear and a house to live in, and to save money for hard days.

And Hashem, blessed be He, commanded His people to rest from all work on the day of Shabbat, and to rest from the work of the field in the seventh year. And the nations of the world wondered how Israel could survive with such hard mitzvot. And Israel, being holy, believed in Hashem and His Torah, overcame their worry and their inclination, and rested on Shabbat and in Shevi'it. And behold, a wonder: no harm or loss befell them; on the contrary, blessing dwelt in their homes, for through the resting they merited to connect to Hashem, the source of blessing. Admittedly, a person was given responsibility to take care of his livelihood, and for this he must lower his eyes to the earth and work the land; but he must also remember the Creator of the world and lift his eyes to heaven, so that beyond his basic existence his work will also have spiritual content, and he will merit to cleave to the Divine, and morality and values will guide him in his work, and blessing will rest on the work of his hands. For this Hashem gave us Shabbat and Shevi'it, so that through them we will be strengthened in faith and connect to His Torah and mitzvot.

And this is what is said (Vayikra 25:18-22): "And you shall do My statutes and keep My ordinances and do them, and you shall dwell in the land in safety. And the land shall yield its fruit, and you shall eat your fill and dwell in safety upon it. And if you shall say: What shall we eat in the seventh year, since we shall not sow nor gather in our produce? Then I will command My blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth produce for the three years. And you shall sow in the eighth year, and eat of the produce, the old store, until the ninth year; until its produce comes in you shall eat the old store."

By contrast, the Sages said: Come and see how severe is the sin of Shevi'it. A person trades in the produce of Shevi'it, and in the end he is forced to sell his movable property. To understand his sin, one must remember that Israel declared their fields ownerless in Shevi'it, and a transgressor who sought easy profits for himself could plunder produce from the fields and trade in it. But since he sinned and became accustomed to profit without working, in the end he will become poor and be forced to sell his movable property. And the Sages continued and said: if he did not awaken to teshuva, in the end he will sell his fields. If he did not repent, he will sell his house. If he did not repent, he will sin by taking a loan with interest, until he is forced to sell himself as a slave (based on Tosefta Arakhin 5:9; Kiddushin 20a).

Even by reason one can understand how the economic situation of those who keep Shabbat and Shevi'it improves compared with those who do not keep them. For although a lack of food is dangerous to a person's existence, lust and the pursuit of honour are more dangerous. Behold, at times a person has a good season and earns a great deal, and in his lust he wastes his profits on luxuries. He could have stored grain and saved money for hard days, but because of his lust and pride he wasted his money. When a hard year comes he will have no bread to give his household and they will die of hunger.

Through resting and refraining from trade in produce, a person rises to deep faith in Hashem and connects to the Torah, and becomes a free man who is able to defer gratification, to master the inclination to lust and laziness, and to be diligent in the six years of work. Out of strengthening his faith a person also becomes content with his lot, and does not need to waste his money on luxuries, and it is easier for him to save, and so he grows steadily richer.

And so the Sages explained that not only the sixth year will be blessed by virtue of the shemita; rather, by virtue of the seventh year the blessing will be drawn from year to year throughout all six years of work (Sifra Behar), in such a way that Israel will learn to plan their work well, and with diligence and efficiency will save grain from year to year, until with correct planning, despite the resting in Shevi'it, they will lack nothing. More than that, from the times in which Israel rest from work and engage in Torah, inspiration will be drawn to the days of action, to invent developments and improvements to make work more efficient and better; and through this a double blessing is drawn from it, for happiness and wealth.2

It is fitting to add that many crises, social and economic, are created following the greed that accompanies the competition in economic and commercial life. A crisis may set the economy back and cause a shortage that lasts several years. The resting in Shevi'it, and the return of the lands and the slaves in the Yovel, dissipate the competition, calm the greed, stop the spiral in the economy, and prevent crises. So it turns out that the seeming loss in Shevi'it is smaller than the gain in preventing economic crises (this will be explained below 11:8).

notes_en.en: The blessing comes through correct planning in the years before Shevi'it, and so one can understand from Sifra Behar (parasha 3, 4:6): "'Then I will command My blessing upon you in the sixth year' – I have only the sixth; from where do we know the fifth, the fourth, the third and the second (and the first)? From where do we know from one year to the next? Scripture says 'and in the year'." Rabbi Pinḥas, author of the 'Hafla'a', explained in 'Panim Yafot' (Vayikra 25:21) that the meaning is that every year the land gave produce greater by a sixth than their needs, and this sixth they would save and keep for the seventh year. And this is the trait of Shammai, as explained in Beitza 16a, who would keep good foods for Shabbat from Sunday. And this is the fitting conduct for a rich man, to plan his deeds and his business well. But Hillel would not save for Shabbat, but trusted that Hashem would provide him on Friday with good foods for Shabbat; and this is the conduct of the poor, who must rely on Hashem. Thus far his words. As is known, the blessing of the Torah is that Israel will live as the rich. And so it was ruled in the laws of Shabbat that the custom fitting for the public is according to the trait of Shammai (MB 250:2; Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 2:1). And see 'Kara Shemita' pp. 62-65. And further see Bava Batra 90b.

sections.title_en: 9. The Mitzva of Shevi'it by Torah Law
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of Shevi'it by Torah law applies when the whole people of Israel dwells on its land as it should, each tribe in its inheritance and each family on its land (Arakhin 32b). As it is said (Vayikra 25:1-3): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe on Mount Sinai, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall rest a Sabbath to the Lord. Six years you shall sow your field, and six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its produce." The Sages expounded (Sifra there): "'Your field' – that each and every one should recognise his field; 'your vineyard' – that each and every one should recognise his vineyard." Therefore, only fourteen years after Israel entered the Land under the leadership of Yehoshua bin Nun did they begin to count years for Shevi'it and Yovel. For seven years they were occupied with conquering the Land and another seven years they were occupied with dividing the inheritances to the tribes and families; and only when they finished dividing the Land did they become obligated in the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel and begin to count years for them (Arakhin 13a; Rambam, Shemita Ve-Yovel 10:2; below 5:1).

Even if all Israel were dwelling in their Land but were mixed with one another – members of the tribe of Binyamin dwelling in the inheritance of Yehuda and members of the tribe of Yehuda in the inheritance of Binyamin – they are not considered as dwelling on the land as they should, and the Torah obligation of Shevi'it is cancelled. Thus the mitzva of Shevi'it depends on the Yovel, for in the Yovel all the inheritances returned to their owners, and by virtue of this all Israel dwelt on their land as they should (Arakhin 32b).

The logic of the mitzva is understandable: only when all Israel have land in the Land and all keep Shevi'it together can they cope with the great challenge of Shevi'it. But when only some have lands, they cannot bear the burden of Shevi'it alone. And even if economically they could rest, it is hard for them to overcome their inclination when the obligation is not placed on everyone equally. Not only that, but each tribe must dwell in its inheritance, for the members of a tribe are better able to help one another withstand the great challenge of resting, and will also take care to enforce the Yovel, in which the lands return to their owners; for one who refuses to return the land he bought harms one of the members of his own tribe. In addition, when not all Israel dwell in the Land, presumably the empty places are filled with foreigners who work their fields all seven years, and create competition that those who keep Shevi'it find it hard to withstand.

Also what is said in the Torah, that Hashem will give His blessing, is fulfilled at a time when all Israel are in their Land and the obligation of Shevi'it is by Torah law (Sma, ḤM 67:2; Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 29:3; Igrot Ha-Re'aya 555; below 7, note 9). For the blessing does not come by way of miracle but by way of nature; and therefore when the realistic conditions do not allow blessing, the blessing departs, for it will not come by way of a miracle.

However, the Sages enacted that even when the obligation of the mitzva by Torah law is cancelled, Israel should keep Shevi'it. But since its obligation is only rabbinic, one does not rely in it on the Divine blessing, and in a pressing situation one is more lenient in it, as will be explained below.

sections.title_en: 10. The People, the Land and Shevi'it
sections.body_en:
In keeping Shevi'it and Yovel the people of Israel merits to reach the peak of completeness in revealing the word of Hashem throughout the whole Land, in the practical life of the individual and of the community together. Therefore the keeping of Shevi'it and Yovel is the foundation for the revelation of the Shekhina in the Land through prophecy, the monarchy, the Temple and the Great Beit Din. Therefore too the Torah emphasised in a special way that these mitzvot were said to Moshe at Sinai, as it is said (Vayikra 25:1-2): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe on Mount Sinai, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall rest a Sabbath to the Lord." The Sages said (Sifra there): from the fact that we learned that the general rules and fine details of the mitzva of Shevi'it were said to Moshe at Sinai, we learned that all the mitzvot too, their general rules and fine details, are from Sinai. For the whole Torah, like the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel, is meant to reveal holiness in the Land.

And since through the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel the people of Israel fulfils its destiny in revealing the Shekhina in the Land, when Israel sin and desecrate Shevi'it, the punishment for it is most severe: Israel are exiled from their Land, and the Land remains bereft and desolate. As it is said (Vayikra 26:32-35): "And I will make the land desolate, and your enemies who dwell in it shall be astonished at it. And you I will scatter among the nations, and I will draw out the sword after you; and your land shall be a desolation and your cities shall be a ruin. Then the land shall be paid its Sabbaths all the days of its desolation, while you are in the land of your enemies; then the land shall rest and pay its Sabbaths. All the days of its desolation it shall rest the rest that it did not have in your Sabbaths when you dwelt upon it."

In practice, it was not easy for the people of Israel to withstand this great challenge. Presumably there were righteous people who always kept Shevi'it, but for many years many of Israel did not keep Shevi'it and Yovel, until about seven hundred years after Israel entered the Land the king of Assyria began to exile the tribes of Israel from the Land, and the Torah obligation of the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel lapsed. At first the tribes that dwelt in Transjordan were exiled. And when Israel did not repent, the other tribes of the Kingdom of Israel were also exiled. And when they did not repent, the Temple was destroyed and the tribes of Yehuda, Binyamin and Levi too were exiled. The Sages said that the seventy years that Israel were exiled to Babylon were on account of the seventy years of shemita and Yovel that they did not keep (Rashi, Vayikra 26:35). The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: "I told you to sow six and release one to Me, so that you would know that the land is Mine; and you did not do so. Rather, get up and be exiled from it, and it will release by itself all the releases that it owes Me" (Sifra Beḥukotai, parasha 2, 7; and likewise in Avot 5:9; Sanhedrin 39a).

Even after the Second Temple was built, the Torah obligation of the mitzva of Shevi'it did not return, because not all Israel returned to the Land, nor did all of them dwell on their land as they should. But the Sages enacted that they should keep the mitzva of Shevi'it by their authority (below 5:3, note 2; 5:5).

It turns out that the years in which Israel kept the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel by Torah law were not in vain: in them the great vision was fixed in the hearts of Israel, and by its power Israel continued for many generations to keep the mitzva by rabbinic law. And more than this, by the power of the great vision, despite the long and terrible exile, the people of Israel continued to dream of the return of Israel to their Land, in order to keep Shevi'it and Yovel in it and to bring redemption to the world.

sections.title_en: 11. The Mitzva in Our Time and in the Future
sections.body_en:
The view of most poskim, and so it is accepted to rule, is that the mitzva of Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, since not all Israel dwell on their land as they should. Admittedly, some Rishonim hold that today there is no obligation to keep Shevi'it, because about three hundred years after the destruction of the Second Temple the Great Beit Din, which sanctified months, intercalated years and counted Yovels, ceased; and in their view, as long as the beit din counted years for the Yovels according to the instruction of the Sages, there was also a rabbinic mitzva to keep Shevi'it, and from the time the beit din ceased and years are not counted, the mitzva of Shevi'it too lapsed, and only as a measure of piety do some keep it (below 5:6).

During the long exile, for many generations there were no Jewish farmers in the Land; and from the time that, by the kindness of Hashem, Israel began to gather to their Land and work their soil, great difficulty arose for the farmers to rest in Shevi'it. The leaders of the settlement too came to realise that resting in Shevi'it could greatly harm the settlement and delay the process of the ingathering of the exiles. In response to this, the great rabbis ruled to remove the obligation of the mitzva of Shevi'it by selling the fields to a non-Jew. And although there were important rabbis who opposed the permit, all the great rabbis of the Land, the local authorities, ruled to permit it, in order to sustain the farmers and to continue the building of the Land and the ingathering of the exiles; for through this we will merit to draw closer to the time when all Israel will dwell on their land as they should, and we will keep the mitzva of Shevi'it as required by Torah law. And this is the well-known 'heter mekhira', which will be explained below in chapter 7. However, the rabbis ruled not to sell ornamental gardens, in order to keep the resting in them as the halakha requires.

Some hold that 'otzar beit din' is the right solution for keeping Shevi'it in our time, without harming Israeli agriculture and without selling the lands into the hands of non-Jews. But as will be explained in chapter 8, this solution can help only partially, because usually its implementation involves prohibitions of work and prohibitions of trade.

It is fitting to advance gradually towards full keeping of Shevi'it, by setting a state budget that will encourage farmers to rest while receiving compensation for every dunam that lies fallow. And in the meantime, every farmer who feels it is hard to rest – it is better that he work within the framework of the 'heter mekhira' than choose another profession. For work in the Land of Israel is a Torah mitzva, and it is preferable tenfold to the wish to be stringent and avoid the 'heter mekhira' (as explained below 7:12; 11:1).

As for consumers, the main produce that is right to consume in Shevi'it is produce grown within the framework of the 'heter mekhira'. And it should be preferred over produce grown by non-Jews. When produce of 'otzar beit din' is distributed for a significantly cheaper payment, there is a beautification of the mitzva in buying it (below 9:1-3).

When all Israel return to the Land and dwell in it as they should, each tribe in its inheritance and each family on its land, we will return to keeping the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel by Torah law (Rambam, Shemita Ve-Yovel 12:16; below 5, note 3). And this will happen in the days of the King Messiah, when by prophecy and the Great Beit Din Israel's lineage will again be traced to their tribes, and the whole Land will be divided among all the families of Israel and the converts who joined Israel in their days of distress (Yeḥezkel 47:13-23; Rambam, Melakhim 12:3; below 11:5).
